claim: Pain is the most prominent symptom of osteoarthritis (OA) progression.
source: Pain is the most prominent symptom of osteoarthritis (OA) progression.
evidence: This is a general statement about OA that draws from established medical knowledge about the disease.

claim: Osteoblasts secrete prostaglandin E2 (PGE2) during aberrant subchondral bone remodeling in mice.
source: Here we report osteoblast secret prostaglandin E2 (PGE2) during aberrant subchondral bone remodeling induces pain and OA progression in mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, including immunostaining showing Cox2 expression in osteocalcin positive osteoblastic cells and PGE2 concentration measurements.

claim: PGE2 secreted by osteoblasts during aberrant subchondral bone remodeling induces pain in mice.
source: Here we report osteoblast secret prostaglandin E2 (PGE2) during aberrant subchondral bone remodeling induces pain and OA progression in mice.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral tests (Von Frey, Catwalk) showing pain reduction when Cox2 is deleted in osteoblasts.

claim: PGE2 secreted by osteoblasts during aberrant subchondral bone remodeling induces OA progression in mice.
source: Here we report osteoblast secret prostaglandin E2 (PGE2) during aberrant subchondral bone remodeling induces pain and OA progression in mice.
evidence: This is supported by histological data showing cartilage degeneration and OARSI scores in the experimental models.

claim: Specific deletion of cyclooxygenase 2 (COX2) in osteoblasts markedly ameliorates OA symptoms in mice.
source: Specific deletion of the major PGE2 producing enzyme cyclooxygenase 2 (COX2) in osteoblasts or PGE2 receptor EP4 in peripheral nerve markedly ameliorates OA symptoms.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Bglap-Cre::Cox2fl/fl mice showing reduced pain behaviors and improved OA outcomes.

claim: Specific deletion of PGE2 receptor EP4 in peripheral nerve markedly ameliorates OA symptoms in mice.
source: Specific deletion of the major PGE2 producing enzyme cyclooxygenase 2 (COX2) in osteoblasts or PGE2 receptor EP4 in peripheral nerve markedly ameliorates OA symptoms.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Avil-Cre::Ptger4fl/fl mice showing reduced pain behaviors and improved OA outcomes.

claim: COX2 is the major PGE2 producing enzyme.
source: Specific deletion of the major PGE2 producing enzyme cyclooxygenase 2 (COX2) in osteoblasts or PGE2 receptor EP4 in peripheral nerve markedly ameliorates OA symptoms.
evidence: This is based on established biochemical knowledge about the role of COX2 in PGE2 synthesis.

claim: PGE2 sensitizes dorsal root ganglia (DRG) neurons by modifying the voltage-gated sodium channel NaV1.8.
source: Mechanistically, PGE2 sensitizes dorsal root ganglia (DRG) neurons by modifying the voltage-gated sodium channel NaV1.8, evidenced by that genetically or pharmacologically inhibiting NaV1.8 in DRG neurons can substantially attenuate OA.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data, immunostaining showing increased NaV1.8 expression, and behavioral data from genetic and pharmacological inhibition experiments.

claim: Genetically inhibiting NaV1.8 in DRG neurons can substantially attenuate OA.
source: Mechanistically, PGE2 sensitizes dorsal root ganglia (DRG) neurons by modifying the voltage-gated sodium channel NaV1.8, evidenced by that genetically or pharmacologically inhibiting NaV1.8 in DRG neurons can substantially attenuate OA.
evidence: This is supported by data from Scn10a-Cre::Rosa26iDTRfl/fl mice showing reduced pain behaviors.

claim: Pharmacologically inhibiting NaV1.8 in DRG neurons can substantially attenuate OA.
source: Mechanistically, PGE2 sensitizes dorsal root ganglia (DRG) neurons by modifying the voltage-gated sodium channel NaV1.8, evidenced by that genetically or pharmacologically inhibiting NaV1.8 in DRG neurons can substantially attenuate OA.
evidence: This is supported by data showing that administration of NaV1.8 inhibitor A-803467 reduced DRG neuronal excitability.

claim: Drugs targeting aberrant subchondral bone remodeling attenuate OA through rebalancing PGE2 production and NaV1.8 modification.
source: Moreover, drugs targeting aberrant subchondral bone remodeling also attenuates OA through rebalancing PGE2 production and NaV1.8 modification.
evidence: This is supported by data from the alendronate-TβR1I conjugate treatment showing improved bone structure, reduced PGE2, decreased NaV1.8 expression, and reduced pain.

claim: Aberrant subchondral remodeling induced NaV1.8 neuronal modification is an important player in OA.
source: Thus, aberrant subchondral remodeling induced NaV1.8 neuronal modification is an important player in OA and is a potential therapeutic target in multiple skeletal degenerative diseases.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the multiple lines of experimental evidence presented in the manuscript.

claim: Aberrant subchondral remodeling induced NaV1.8 neuronal modification is a potential therapeutic target in multiple skeletal degenerative diseases.
source: Thus, aberrant subchondral remodeling induced NaV1.8 neuronal modification is an important player in OA and is a potential therapeutic target in multiple skeletal degenerative diseases.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential therapeutic applications based on the findings.

claim: Subchondral bone absorbs compressive forces during movement.
source: Subchondral bone is an integral component of the joint, absorbing compressive forces during movement (Martel-Pelletier et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Physiological subchondral bone remodeling maintains structural integrity and supports the overlying articular cartilage.
source: Physiological subchondral bone remodeling maintains its structural integrity and supports the overlying articular cartilage.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about bone physiology.

claim: Age or trauma related alteration of subchondral bone is a principal risk factor of osteoarthritis.
source: Age or trauma (Hayami et al., 2004) related alteration of subchondral bone is a principal risk factor of osteoarthritis (OA), the most common joint disease (Berenbaum et al., 2018) characterized by cartilage destruction (Glasson et al., 2005; Kim et al., 2014a), subchondral sclerosis (Suri et al., 2007) and synovitis (Benito et al., 2005; Sellam and Berenbaum, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: OA is the most common joint disease.
source: Age or trauma (Hayami et al., 2004) related alteration of subchondral bone is a principal risk factor of osteoarthritis (OA), the most common joint disease (Berenbaum et al., 2018) characterized by cartilage destruction (Glasson et al., 2005; Kim et al., 2014a), subchondral sclerosis (Suri et al., 2007) and synovitis (Benito et al., 2005; Sellam and Berenbaum, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: OA is characterized by cartilage destruction.
source: Age or trauma (Hayami et al., 2004) related alteration of subchondral bone is a principal risk factor of osteoarthritis (OA), the most common joint disease (Berenbaum et al., 2018) characterized by cartilage destruction (Glasson et al., 2005; Kim et al., 2014a), subchondral sclerosis (Suri et al., 2007) and synovitis (Benito et al., 2005; Sellam and Berenbaum, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: OA is characterized by subchondral sclerosis.
source: Age or trauma (Hayami et al., 2004) related alteration of subchondral bone is a principal risk factor of osteoarthritis (OA), the most common joint disease (Berenbaum et al., 2018) characterized by cartilage destruction (Glasson et al., 2005; Kim et al., 2014a), subchondral sclerosis (Suri et al., 2007) and synovitis (Benito et al., 2005; Sellam and Berenbaum, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: OA is characterized by synovitis.
source: Age or trauma (Hayami et al., 2004) related alteration of subchondral bone is a principal risk factor of osteoarthritis (OA), the most common joint disease (Berenbaum et al., 2018) characterized by cartilage destruction (Glasson et al., 2005; Kim et al., 2014a), subchondral sclerosis (Suri et al., 2007) and synovitis (Benito et al., 2005; Sellam and Berenbaum, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Pain is the major symptom for OA patients.
source: Pain, as the major symptom for OA patients (Lane et al., 2010), often leads to physical disability and mortality in senior patients (Chen et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: OA pain often leads to physical disability and mortality in senior patients.
source: Pain, as the major symptom for OA patients (Lane et al., 2010), often leads to physical disability and mortality in senior patients (Chen et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The major local source of OA pain is not clearly defined.
source: Although the major local source is not clearly defined (Malfait and Schnitzer, 2013), there is evidence showing that synovitis (Sellam and Berenbaum, 2010) and subchondral bone marrow lesion (BML) are highly relevant to OA pain.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Synovitis is highly relevant to OA pain.
source: Although the major local source is not clearly defined (Malfait and Schnitzer, 2013), there is evidence showing that synovitis (Sellam and Berenbaum, 2010) and subchondral bone marrow lesion (BML) are highly relevant to OA pain.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Subchondral bone marrow lesion (BML) is highly relevant to OA pain.
source: Although the major local source is not clearly defined (Malfait and Schnitzer, 2013), there is evidence showing that synovitis (Sellam and Berenbaum, 2010) and subchondral bone marrow lesion (BML) are highly relevant to OA pain.
evidence: This is supported by the citation and the manuscript's own data.

claim: BML is a fluid enriched area under magnetic resonance imaging (MRI).
source: BML is a fluid enriched area under magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and is characterized as bone marrow edema, fibrosis, microfractures or trabecular pattern alterations in pathological examinations, with high relevance to abnormal bone remodeling.
evidence: This is based on established radiological and pathological knowledge.

claim: BML is characterized as bone marrow edema, fibrosis, microfractures or trabecular pattern alterations in pathological examinations.
source: BML is a fluid enriched area under magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and is characterized as bone marrow edema, fibrosis, microfractures or trabecular pattern alterations in pathological examinations, with high relevance to abnormal bone remodeling.
evidence: This is based on established pathological knowledge.

claim: BML has high relevance to abnormal bone remodeling.
source: BML is a fluid enriched area under magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and is characterized as bone marrow edema, fibrosis, microfractures or trabecular pattern alterations in pathological examinations, with high relevance to abnormal bone remodeling.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge and supported by the manuscript's findings.

claim: Aberrant subchondral bone remodeling in response to altered mechanical loading patterns in OA was initiated by over-activation of transforming growth factor β1 (TGF-β1).
source: We previously showed that aberrant subchondral bone remodeling in response to altered mechanical loading patterns in OA was initiated by over-activation of transforming growth factor β1 (TGF-β1).
evidence: This refers to the authors' previous published work.

claim: High levels of subchondral TGF-β1 signaling induces mesenchymal stem cells (MSC) clustering.
source: High levels of subchondral TGF-β1 signaling induces mesenchymal stem cells (MSC) clustering and leads to the uncoupling of osteoblastic bone formation, osteoclastic bone resorption and angiogenesis.
evidence: This refers to the authors' previous findings.

claim: High levels of subchondral TGF-β1 signaling leads to the uncoupling of osteoblastic bone formation, osteoclastic bone resorption and angiogenesis.
source: High levels of subchondral TGF-β1 signaling induces mesenchymal stem cells (MSC) clustering and leads to the uncoupling of osteoblastic bone formation, osteoclastic bone resorption and angiogenesis.
evidence: This refers to the authors' previous findings.

claim: Overactivated osteoclasts in BML aggravated OA pain by secreting the axon guidance molecule Netrin-1 to induce subchondral sensory innervation.
source: Moreover, we found overactivated osteoclasts in BML aggravated OA pain by secreting the axon guidance molecule Netrin-1 to induce subchondral sensory innervation (Zhu et al., 2019).
evidence: This refers to the authors' previous published work.

claim: Increased sensory innervation provides a structural base for the transmission of nociceptive signals from the subchondral bone to the central nervous system.
source: The increased sensory innervation provides a structural base for the transmission of nociceptive signals from the subchondral bone to the central nervous system.
evidence: This is an inference based on neurobiological principles and the authors' findings.

claim: Persistent low grade of local inflammation is a hallmark of OA.
source: The persistent low grade of local inflammation is another hallmark of OA (Midwood et al., 2009; Tu et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: During the uncoupled bone remodeling in OA progression, a series of pro-inflammatory factors like prostaglandin E2 (PGE2), interleukin-1β (IL-1β), interleukin-6 (IL-6) are released into the subchondral bone area.
source: During the uncoupled bone remodeling in OA progression, a series of pro-inflammatory factors (Kapoor et al., 2011; Sellam and Berenbaum, 2010) like prostaglandin E2 (PGE2) (Chen et al., 2019), interleukin-1β (IL-1β), interleukin-6 (IL-6) are released into the subchondral bone area (Massicotte et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: PGE2 is a crucial factor in both pain sensation and bone metabolism.
source: We previously showed that PGE2 was a crucial factor in both pain sensation and bone metabolism (Tu et al., 2019).
evidence: This refers to the authors' previous published work.

claim: Sensory nerves monitor bone density by responding to the concentration of PGE2 in bone.
source: PGE2 concentration is inversely related to bone mass and sensory nerves monitors bone density by responding to the concentration of PGE2 in bone (Chen et al., 2019).
evidence: This refers to the authors' previous published work.

claim: PGE2 concentration is inversely related to bone mass.
source: PGE2 concentration is inversely related to bone mass and sensory nerves monitors bone density by responding to the concentration of PGE2 in bone (Chen et al., 2019).
evidence: This refers to the authors' previous published work.

claim: When bone mass is decreased, the enzymatic activity of cyclooxygenase 2 (Cox2) in osteoblastic lineage cells is significantly increased.
source: We found that when bone mass is decreased, the enzymatic activity of cyclooxygenase 2 (Cox2) in osteoblastic lineage cells was significantly increased and thus catalyzes more arachidonic acid into PGE2.
evidence: This refers to the authors' previous findings.

claim: Increased Cox2 activity catalyzes more arachidonic acid into PGE2.
source: We found that when bone mass is decreased, the enzymatic activity of cyclooxygenase 2 (Cox2) in osteoblastic lineage cells was significantly increased and thus catalyzes more arachidonic acid into PGE2.
evidence: This is based on established biochemical knowledge about Cox2 function.

claim: At the early stage of OA, the bone density is temporarily decreased.
source: At the early stage of OA, the bone density is temporarily decreased, which resembles the low bone density as seen in osteoporosis.
evidence: This is supported by the manuscript's own data showing decreased bone density at early OA stages.

claim: The early stage of OA resembles the low bone density as seen in osteoporosis.
source: At the early stage of OA, the bone density is temporarily decreased, which resembles the low bone density as seen in osteoporosis.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of bone density patterns.

claim: PGE2 functions as an inflammatory mediator.
source: PGE2 functions as an inflammatory mediator and a neuromodulator that alters neuronal excitability (Samad et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: PGE2 functions as a neuromodulator that alters neuronal excitability.
source: PGE2 functions as an inflammatory mediator and a neuromodulator that alters neuronal excitability (Samad et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: EP4 receptor is the primary mediator of PGE2-evoked inflammatory pain hypersensitivity and sensitization of sensory neurons.
source: In the four types of G-protein-coupled EP receptors (EP1-EP4) that mediate the functions of PGE2, EP4 receptor is considered as the primary mediator of PGE2- evoked inflammatory pain hypersensitivity and sensitization of sensory neurons (Boyd et al., 2011; Chen et al., 2008; Lin et al., 2006; McCoy et al., 2002; Nakao et al., 2007; Southall and Vasko, 2001; Taylor-Clark et al., 2008), as evidenced by that the specific EP4 receptor antagonists could reduce acute and chronic pain (Nakao et al., 2007), including OA pain (Abdel-Magid, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Specific EP4 receptor antagonists could reduce acute and chronic pain.
source: In the four types of G-protein-coupled EP receptors (EP1-EP4) that mediate the functions of PGE2, EP4 receptor is considered as the primary mediator of PGE2- evoked inflammatory pain hypersensitivity and sensitization of sensory neurons (Boyd et al., 2011; Chen et al., 2008; Lin et al., 2006; McCoy et al., 2002; Nakao et al., 2007; Southall and Vasko, 2001; Taylor-Clark et al., 2008), as evidenced by that the specific EP4 receptor antagonists could reduce acute and chronic pain (Nakao et al., 2007), including OA pain (Abdel-Magid, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Specific EP4 receptor antagonists could reduce OA pain.
source: In the four types of G-protein-coupled EP receptors (EP1-EP4) that mediate the functions of PGE2, EP4 receptor is considered as the primary mediator of PGE2- evoked inflammatory pain hypersensitivity and sensitization of sensory neurons (Boyd et al., 2011; Chen et al., 2008; Lin et al., 2006; McCoy et al., 2002; Nakao et al., 2007; Southall and Vasko, 2001; Taylor-Clark et al., 2008), as evidenced by that the specific EP4 receptor antagonists could reduce acute and chronic pain (Nakao et al., 2007), including OA pain (Abdel-Magid, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Increased neuronal excitability contributes to the generation of hypersensitivity in various types of chronic pain.
source: Increased neuronal excitability contributes to the generation of hypersensitivity in various types of chronic pain (Kuner, 2010; Malfait and Schnitzer, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: PGE2 potentiates several ion channels in neurons to enhance neuronal excitability.
source: PGE2 has been shown to potentiate several ion channels in neurons to enhance neuronal excitability (Funk, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Voltage-gated sodium channel (NaV) is a member of the tetrodotoxin-resistant sodium channel (TTX-R).
source: Voltage-gated sodium channel (NaV), a member of the tetrodotoxin-resistant sodium channel (TTX-R), is mainly expressed in small- and medium-sized Dorsal root ganglion (DRG) neurons and their fibers.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about sodium channel classification.

claim: NaV is mainly expressed in small- and medium-sized Dorsal root ganglion (DRG) neurons and their fibers.
source: Voltage-gated sodium channel (NaV), a member of the tetrodotoxin-resistant sodium channel (TTX-R), is mainly expressed in small- and medium-sized Dorsal root ganglion (DRG) neurons and their fibers.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about NaV expression patterns.

claim: NaV is responsible for initiating and propagating electrical signal transmission by inducing Na+ influx to start action potential firing.
source: The NaV is responsible for initiating and propagating electrical signal transmission by inducing Na+ influx to start action potential firing.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about sodium channel function.

claim: PGE2 modulates the sodium current of the TTX-R in DRG neurons.
source: PGE2 has been shown to modulate the sodium current of the TTX-R in DRG neurons and promote Nav1.8 trafficking to the cell surface (England et al., 1996; Liu et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: PGE2 promotes Nav1.8 trafficking to the cell surface.
source: PGE2 has been shown to modulate the sodium current of the TTX-R in DRG neurons and promote Nav1.8 trafficking to the cell surface (England et al., 1996; Liu et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: NaV1.8 is the main drug target among the 9 subtypes of NaVs due to its high relevance to pain signal transmission.
source: Among the 9 subtypes of NaVs (NaV1.1–1.9), NaV1.8 (Akopian et al., 1996) is the main drug target due to its highly relevant to pain signal transmission, and restricted distribution in primary nociceptive neurons (Akopian et al., 1999; Julius and Basbaum, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: NaV1.8 has restricted distribution in primary nociceptive neurons.
source: Among the 9 subtypes of NaVs (NaV1.1–1.9), NaV1.8 (Akopian et al., 1996) is the main drug target due to its highly relevant to pain signal transmission, and restricted distribution in primary nociceptive neurons (Akopian et al., 1999; Julius and Basbaum, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Gain of function mutations in the promoter region of NaV1.8 directly induces pain hypersensitivity in humans.
source: Gain of function mutations in human in the promoter region of NaV1.8 directly induces pain hypersensitivity (Duan et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Animals lacking NaV1.8 display significantly lower mechanical pain sensitivity with modest changes in heat or innocuous touch sensitivities.
source: Interestingly, animals lacking NaV1.8 display significant lower mechanical pain sensitivity with modest changes in heat or innocuous touch sensitivities (Akopian et al., 1999; Basbaum et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Post-transcriptional modifications of NaV1.8 including phosphorylation and methylglyoxalation regulate its activity.
source: Moreover, post-transcriptional modifications of NaV1.8 including phosphorylation (Gold et al., 1998; Hudmon et al., 2008; Wu et al., 2012) and methylglyoxalation (Bierhaus et al., 2012) further regulate its activity.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Inhibition of the expression of NaVs in nociceptive neurons was effective in OA pain alleviation.
source: A recent study demonstrated that inhibition of the expression of NaVs in nociceptive neurons was effective in OA pain alleviation (Miller et al., 2017), with the detailed molecular mechanism remained to be clarified (Strickland et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The expression of mRNA encoding NaV1.8 increased 2.5 folds in the ACLT group as the highest upregulation among all the NaVs.
source: Compares to the sham-operated group, the expression of mRNA encoding NaV1.8 increased 2.5 folds in the ACLT group as the highest upregulation among all the NaVs.
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The mRNAs encoding NaV1.7 and NaV1.9 showed moderate upregulation in the ACLT group relative to that of the Sham group.
source: The mRNAs encoding NaV1.7 and NaV1.9 showed moderate upregulation in the ACLT group relative to that of the Sham group while the changes of NaV1.1 NaV1.2 NaV1.3 or NaV1.6 were not detected (Figure 1a).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1a.

claim: The changes of NaV1.1 NaV1.2 NaV1.3 or NaV1.6 were not detected in ACLT mice compared to sham.
source: The mRNAs encoding NaV1.7 and NaV1.9 showed moderate upregulation in the ACLT group relative to that of the Sham group while the changes of NaV1.1 NaV1.2 NaV1.3 or NaV1.6 were not detected (Figure 1a).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1a.

claim: The intensity of NaV1.8 immunofluorescence in subchondral bone was elevated about 2 to 3 folds in OA mice compared to sham-operated mice one- or two-months post-surgery.
source: The intensity of NaV1.8 immunofluorescence in subchondral bone was also elevated about 2 to 3 folds in OA mice compared to sham- operated mice one- or two-months post-surgery (Figure 1b and c).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1b and c.

claim: The expression rate of NaV1.8 in total nerve fibers innervated in subchondral bone significantly increased post-ACLT.
source: The expression rate of NaV1.8 in total nerve fibers (labeled by pan neuron marker PGP9.5) innervated in subchondral bone significantly increased post-ACLT (Figure 1—figure supplement 1a,f).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1a,f.

claim: The elevated NaV1.8 expression was highly co-localized with the peptidergic nociceptor marked by calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP).
source: Moreover, the elevated NaV1.8 expression was highly co-localized with the peptidergic nociceptor marked by calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP) (Brain et al., 1985; Figure 1—figure supplement 1b,f) and mechanosensitive low-threshold mechanoceptors (labeled by PIEZO2) (Eijkelkamp et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by co-immunostaining data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1b,f.

claim: The elevated NaV1.8 expression was highly co-localized with mechanosensitive low-threshold mechanoceptors (labeled by PIEZO2).
source: Moreover, the elevated NaV1.8 expression was highly co-localized with the peptidergic nociceptor marked by calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP) (Brain et al., 1985; Figure 1—figure supplement 1b,f) and mechanosensitive low-threshold mechanoceptors (labeled by PIEZO2) (Eijkelkamp et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by co-immunostaining data and a citation.

claim: Western blot analysis of ipsilateral lumbar 3–5 DRG confirmed the upregulation of NaV1.8 expression at the DRG level.
source: Both western blot analysis (Figure 1f) and immunostaining (Figure 1—figure supplement 1f 1 g, i) of ipsilateral lumbar 3–5 DRG confirmed the upregulation of NaV1.8 expression at the DRG level.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1f.

claim: Immunostaining of ipsilateral lumbar 3–5 DRG confirmed the upregulation of NaV1.8 expression at the DRG level.
source: Both western blot analysis (Figure 1f) and immunostaining (Figure 1—figure supplement 1f 1 g, i) of ipsilateral lumbar 3–5 DRG confirmed the upregulation of NaV1.8 expression at the DRG level.
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1f 1 g, i.

claim: The NaV1.8+ neurons labeled by DiI significantly increased in the DRG neurons of OA rats relative to sham-operated rats.
source: We found that the NaV1.8+ neurons labeled by DiI significantly increased in the DRG neurons of OA rats relative to sham-operated rats (Figure 1g,h), indicating that DiI was transported into DRG neurons by the sensory fibers innervated subchondral bone in a retrograde manner.
evidence: This is supported by retrograde tracing data shown in Figure 1g,h.

claim: DiI was transported into DRG neurons by the sensory fibers innervated subchondral bone in a retrograde manner.
source: We found that the NaV1.8+ neurons labeled by DiI significantly increased in the DRG neurons of OA rats relative to sham-operated rats (Figure 1g,h), indicating that DiI was transported into DRG neurons by the sensory fibers innervated subchondral bone in a retrograde manner.
evidence: This is an inference based on the retrograde tracing experimental design and results.

claim: The hind paw withdrawal threshold (HPWT) dropped nearly 60% and maintained at this level throughout the two month-period post ACLT relative to the sham-operated group.
source: Von Frey test showed that the hind paw withdrawal threshold (HPWT) dropped nearly 60% and maintained at this level throughout the two month-period post ACLT relative to the sham-operated group, suggesting that development of mechanical allodynia in OA mice (Figure 1g; Chen et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by Von Frey test data shown in Figure 1g.

claim: The number of excited DRG neurons ipsilateral to the surgery significantly increased in OA mice compared to sham-operated mice.
source: The number of excited DRG neurons ipsilateral to the surgery significantly increased in OA mice compared to sham-operated mice, and importantly, administration of NaV1.8 inhibitor (A-803467)(Jarvis et al., 2007) blunted the signal in DRG (Figure 1h and i).
evidence: This is supported by in vivo DRG imaging data shown in Figure 1h and i.

claim: Administration of NaV1.8 inhibitor (A-803467) blunted the signal in DRG.
source: The number of excited DRG neurons ipsilateral to the surgery significantly increased in OA mice compared to sham-operated mice, and importantly, administration of NaV1.8 inhibitor (A-803467)(Jarvis et al., 2007) blunted the signal in DRG (Figure 1h and i).
evidence: This is supported by in vivo DRG imaging data shown in Figure 1h and i.

claim: The action potential number significantly elevated in ACLT mice relative to sham-operated mice.
source: The action potential number and NaV1.8 current density significantly elevated in ACLT mice relative to sham-operated mice, and the elevations were blocked by A-803467 (Figure 1j–l, Figure 1—figure supplement 1f 1 k and l).
evidence: This is supported by patch-clamp data shown in Figure 1j–l.

claim: NaV1.8 current density significantly elevated in ACLT mice relative to sham-operated mice.
source: The action potential number and NaV1.8 current density significantly elevated in ACLT mice relative to sham-operated mice, and the elevations were blocked by A-803467 (Figure 1j–l, Figure 1—figure supplement 1f 1 k and l).
evidence: This is supported by patch-clamp data shown in Figure 1j–l.

claim: The elevations of action potential number and NaV1.8 current density were blocked by A-803467.
source: The action potential number and NaV1.8 current density significantly elevated in ACLT mice relative to sham-operated mice, and the elevations were blocked by A-803467 (Figure 1j–l, Figure 1—figure supplement 1f 1 k and l).
evidence: This is supported by patch-clamp data shown in Figure 1j–l.

claim: Cox2 expression was significantly increased in subchondral bone and primarily in osteocalcin positive osteoblastic cells post ACLT mice compared with sham-operated mice.
source: Cox2 expression was significantly increased in subchondral bone and primarily in osteocalcin positive osteoblastic cells post ACLT mice compared with sham-operated mice (Figure 2a and b).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2a and b.

claim: PGE2 concentration in subchondral bone increased about three times in OA mice relative to sham-operated mice.
source: Consistently, PGE2 concentration in subchondral bone increased about three times in OA mice relative to sham-operated mice (Figure 2c, Figure 2—figure supplement 1a–d).
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: PGE2 concentration in subchondral bone was significantly lower in Bglap-Cre::Cox2fl/fl mice compared with Cox2fl/fl mice post ACLT.
source: PGE2 concentration in subchondral bone was significantly lower in Bglap-Cre::Cox2fl/fl mice compared with Cox2fl/fl mice post ACLT (Figure 2h).
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 2h.

claim: The NaV1.8 immunofluorescence intensity in subchondral bone immunostaining was significantly reduced in Bglap-Cre::Cox2fl/fl mice compared with Cox2fl/fl mice.
source: Notably, the NaV1.8 immunofluorescence intensity in subchondral bone immunostaining was also significantly reduced in Bglap-Cre::Cox2fl/fl mice compared with Cox2fl/fl mice (Figure 2d and i).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2d and i.

claim: The number of NaV1.8+ neurons in DRG was significantly decreased in the Bglap-Cre::Cox2fl/fl mice relative to Cox2fl/fl mice.
source: In addition, the number of NaV1.8+ neurons in DRG was also significantly decreased (Figure 2e and j) in the Bglap-Cre::Cox2fl/fl mice relative to Cox2fl/fl mice.
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2e and j.

claim: The number of excited neurons was significantly reduced in Bglap-Cre::Cox2fl/fl::PirtGCaMP3fl/- mice compared with Cox2fl/fl::Pirt GCaMP3fl/- mice post ACLT.
source: Pirt-GCaMP3 DRG imaging showed that the number of excited neurons was significantly reduced in Bglap-Cre::Cox2fl/fl::PirtGCaMP3fl/- mice compared with Cox2fl/fl::Pirt GCaMP3fl/- mice post ACLT (Figure 2f and k).
evidence: This is supported by in vivo DRG imaging data shown in Figure 2f and k.

claim: The action potential firing number was significantly decreased in Bglap-Cre::Cox2fl/fl mice compared with Cox2fl/fl mice after ACLT.
source: The whole cell current clamp revealed that the action potential firing number was significantly decreased in Bglap-Cre::Cox2fl/fl mice compared with Cox2fl/fl mice after ACLT (Figure 2g and l).
evidence: This is supported by patch-clamp data shown in Figure 2g and l.

claim: The NaV1.8 current density was reduced for about 40% in Bglap-Cre::Cox2fl/fl mice compared with Cox2fl/fl mice.
source: Concurrently, the NaV1.8 current density was reduced for about 40% recorded by the whole-cell voltage-clamp (Figure 2g and m).
evidence: This is supported by patch-clamp data shown in Figure 2g and m.

claim: The mechanical allodynia was simultaneously attenuated in Bglap-Cre::Cox2fl/flmice relative to Cox2fl/fl mice as revealed by the Von Frey behavior test.
source: The mechanical allodynia was simultaneously attenuated in Bglap-Cre::Cox2fl/flmice relative to Cox2fl/fl mice as revealed by the Von Frey behavior test (Figure 2n).
evidence: This is supported by Von Frey test data shown in Figure 2n.

claim: The Maximal Contact At and Maximal Intensity of ipsilateral hind paw was significantly higher in Bglap-Cre::Cox2fl/fl mice compared with Cox2fl/fl mice post ACLT.
source: Catwalk analysis also showed that the Maximal Contact At and Maximal Intensity of ipsilateral hind paw was significantly higher in Bglap-Cre::Cox2fl/fl mice compared with Cox2fl/fl mice post ACLT (Figure 2o).
evidence: This is supported by Catwalk analysis data shown in Figure 2o.

claim: NaV1.8 protein expression was significantly reduced by siRNA against EP4 in western blot analysis of DRG neuron lysates.
source: We found that NaV1.8 protein expression was significantly reduced by siRNA against EP4 in western blot analysis of levels from the cell lysates.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data from in vitro experiments.

claim: Knocking-down the expression of EP1-EP3 did not have a significant effect on Nav1.8 expression.
source: Knocking-down the expression of EP1-EP3 did not have a significant effect on Nav1.8 expression (Figure 2—figure supplement 1i).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1i.

claim: The intensity of NaV1.8 immunofluorescence was significantly reduced in Avil-Cre::Ptger4 fl/fl mice compared with Ptger4 fl/fl mice post-ACLT.
source: Consistently with Bglap-Cre::Cox2fl/fl mice, the intensity of NaV1.8 immunofluorescence was significantly reduced in Avil-Cre::Ptger4 fl/fl mice compared with Ptger4 fl/fl mice post-ACLT (Figure 3a,d, Figure 2—figure supplement 1e–h).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3a,d.

claim: In vivo ipsilateral L4 DRG Pirt GCaMP3 imaging demonstrated significantly dampened excitability in the Ptger4 fl/fl:: Pirt - GCaMP3fl/- mice relative to the control group.
source: In vivo ipsilateral L4 DRG Pirt GCaMP3 imaging demonstrated significantly dampened excitability in the Ptger4 fl/fl:: Pirt - GCaMP3fl/- mice relative to the control group (Figure 3b and e).
evidence: This is supported by in vivo DRG imaging data shown in Figure 3b and e.

claim: The DRG neuronal hypersensitivity and NaV1.8 currents were significantly reduced in Avil-Cre::Ptger4 fl/fl mice relative to Ptger4 fl/fl mice post-ACLT.
source: The patch-clamp analysis further revealed that the DRG neuronal hypersensitivity and NaV1.8 currents were significantly reduced in Avil-Cre::Ptger4 fl/fl mice relative to Ptger4 fl/fl mice post-ACLT (Figure 3c,f,g).
evidence: This is supported by patch-clamp data shown in Figure 3c,f,g.

claim: Both Von Frey test and catwalk analysis showed attenuation of OA pain when EP4 is conditionally deleted in sensory neurons.
source: Moreover, both Von Frey test and catwalk analysis showed attenuation of OA pain when EP4 is conditionally deleted in sensory neurons (Figure 3h and i).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral test data shown in Figure 3h and i.

claim: NaV1.8 transcription levels were significantly elevated at 6 and 12 hr after incubation with PGE2.
source: The result showed that NaV1.8 transcription levels were significantly elevated at 6 and 12 hr after incubation with PGE2 (Figure 4a).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 4a.

claim: PGE2 stimulated phosphorylation of protein kinase A (PKA).
source: Moreover, PGE2 stimulated phosphorylation of protein kinase A (PKA) (Gold et al., 1998) and cAMP response element-binding protein (Creb1) (Lonze and Ginty, 2002; Figure 4b).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4b and citations.

claim: PGE2 stimulated phosphorylation of cAMP response element-binding protein (Creb1).
source: Moreover, PGE2 stimulated phosphorylation of protein kinase A (PKA) (Gold et al., 1998) and cAMP response element-binding protein (Creb1) (Lonze and Ginty, 2002; Figure 4b).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4b and citations.

claim: The effect of PGE2 and Forskolin in the upregulation of NaV1.8 protein expression was dampened by Creb1 inhibitor 666–15.
source: Notably, the effect of PGE2 and Forskolin, a cAMP stimulant in the upregulation of NaV1.8 protein expression was dampened by Creb1 inhibitor 666–15 (Figure 4c), indicating PGE2 stimulates Nav1.8 expression through the PKA-Creb1 signaling pathway.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4c.

claim: PGE2 stimulates Nav1.8 expression through the PKA-Creb1 signaling pathway.
source: Notably, the effect of PGE2 and Forskolin, a cAMP stimulant in the upregulation of NaV1.8 protein expression was dampened by Creb1 inhibitor 666–15 (Figure 4c), indicating PGE2 stimulates Nav1.8 expression through the PKA-Creb1 signaling pathway.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing that inhibiting PKA or CREB blocks PGE2's effect.

claim: The neuronal excitability and NaV1.8 current density stimulated by PGE2 was abolished by the application of PKA inhibitor (PKI) or CREB inhibitor 666–15.
source: Consistently, the neuronal excitability and NaV1.8 current density stimulated by PGE2 was abolished by the application of PKA inhibitor (PKI) or CREB inhibitor 666–15 (Figure 4d–f).
evidence: This is supported by patch-clamp data shown in Figure 4d–f.

claim: PKA levels significantly increased in NaV1.8 positive DRG neurons in ACLT mice compared with sham-operated mice.
source: Co-immunofluorescence staining further demonstrated that PKA levels significantly increased in NaV1.8 positive DRG neurons in ACLT mice compared with sham-operated mice (Figure 4g and h).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 4g and h.

claim: pCreb1 binds to the NaV1.8 promoter at binding site two to stimulate transcription of NaV1.8 gene.
source: ChIP assay revealed that pCreb1 binds to the NaV1.8 promoter at binding site two to stimulate transcription of NaV1.8 gene (Figure 4i–k).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP assay data shown in Figure 4i–k.

claim: The ablation of NaV1.8+ neurons had no effect on the articular cartilage deterioration, as shown by similar OARSI scores between Scn10a -Cre:: Rosa26iDTRfl/fl mice and Rosa26iDTRfl/fl mice post-ACLT.
source: The ablation of NaV1.8+ neurons had no effect on the articular cartilage deterioration, as shown by similar OARSI scores between Scn10a -Cre:: Rosa26iDTRfl/fl mice and Rosa26iDTRfl/fl mice post-ACLT (Figure 5a,e).
evidence: This is supported by histological data and OARSI scoring shown in Figure 5a,e.

claim: The efficacy of specific neuron ablation was evidenced by a significant reduction of NaV1.8+ signals at both subchondral bone and DRG level.
source: The efficacy of specific neuron ablation was evidenced by a significant reduction of NaV1.8+ signals at both subchondral bone and DRG level (Figure 5b,c,f,g).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 5b,c,f,g.

claim: The DRG hypersensitivity was reduced as indicated by a decreased AP firing in Scn10a -Cre:: Rosa26iDTRfl/fl mice.
source: Consistently, the DRG hypersensitivity was reduced as indicated by a decreased AP firing (Figure 5d and h).
evidence: This is supported by patch-clamp data shown in Figure 5d and h.

claim: Max intensity was increased in Scn10a -Cre:: Rosa26iDTRfl/fl mice.
source: The results showed that max intensity, which reflected mechanical pain sensitivity (Kameda et al., 2017), was increased in Scn10a -Cre:: Rosa26iDTRfl/fl mice (Figure 5i).
evidence: This is supported by Catwalk analysis data shown in Figure 5i.

claim: The Von Frey test displayed a significant reduction of HPWT in Scn10a -Cre:: Rosa26iDTRfl/fl mice compared with Rosa26iDTRfl/fl mice after ACLT.
source: Similarly, the Von Frey test displayed a significant reduction of HPWT in Scn10a -Cre:: Rosa26iDTRfl/fl mice compared with Rosa26iDTRfl/fl mice after ACLT (Figure 5j).
evidence: This is supported by Von Frey test data shown in Figure 5j.

claim: The articular cartilage degeneration was attenuated with a weekly injection of conjugate 100 ug/kg in ACLT mice compared with the vehicle group.
source: As expected, the articular cartilage degeneration was attenuated with a weekly injection of conjugate 100 ug/kg in ACLT mice compared with the vehicle group, with a significant improvement of the OARSI score (Figure 6a and g).
evidence: This is supported by histological data and OARSI scoring shown in Figure 6a and g.

claim: The subchondral bone microarchitecture was improved in μCT analysis of ACLT mice treated with the conjugate treatment compared with the vehicle group.
source: In concurrent with the cartilage protection, the subchondral bone microarchitecture was improved in μCT analysis of ACLT mice treated with the conjugate treatment compared with the vehicle group (Figure 6b and h, Figure 6—figure supplement 3f).
evidence: This is supported by μCT data shown in Figure 6b and h.

claim: Phosphorylation of Smad2/3 was effectively inhibited by the conjugate in the subchondral bone.
source: As shown in Figure 6c and i, phosphorylation of Smad2/3 was effectively inhibited by the conjugate in the subchondral bone.
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 6c and i.

claim: The number of TRAP+ osteoclastic cells and Osterix+ pre-osteoblast were reduced by conjugate treatment.
source: The number of TRAP+ osteoclastic cells and Osterix+ pre-osteoblast were reduced (Figure 6—figure supplement 3e and g, Figure 6d and j).
evidence: This is supported by histological data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3e and g, Figure 6d and j.

claim: The BML in tibial subchondral bone was significantly reduced in the conjugate treated group.
source: As a result, the BML in tibial subchondral bone was significantly reduced in the conjugate treated group (Figure 6f) further indicating that coupling of the osteoclast bone resorption and osteoblastic bone formation were restored.
evidence: This is supported by MRI data shown in Figure 6f.

claim: Subchondral PGE2 concentration was significantly reduced in ACLT mice with the conjugate treatment relative to the vehicle group.
source: Interestingly, subchondral PGE2 concentration was significantly reduced in ACLT mice with the conjugate treatment relative to the vehicle group (Figure 6l).
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 6l.

claim: The expression of NaV1.8 was reduced in both subchondral bone and ipsilateral lumbar DRG by conjugate treatment.
source: Importantly, the expression of NaV1.8 was also reduced in both subchondral bone (Figure 6e and k), and ipsilateral lumbar DRG (Figure 6m).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining and western blot data shown in Figure 6e, k, and m.

claim: Conjugate treatment blunted the upregulation of DRG neuron activity in ACLT mice.
source: Moreover, the electrophysiological tests demonstrate that data showed that conjugate treatment blunted the upregulation of DRG neuron activity (Figure 6n and o) and NaV1.8 currents (Figure 6n and p) in ACLT mice.
evidence: This is supported by patch-clamp data shown in Figure 6n and o.

claim: Conjugate treatment blunted the upregulation of NaV1.8 currents in ACLT mice.
source: Moreover, the electrophysiological tests demonstrate that data showed that conjugate treatment blunted the upregulation of DRG neuron activity (Figure 6n and o) and NaV1.8 currents (Figure 6n and p) in ACLT mice.
evidence: This is supported by patch-clamp data shown in Figure 6n and p.

claim: HPWT, maximal contact AT and swing phase were significantly ameliorated in ACLT mice with the administration of conjugate relative to the vehicle group.
source: The effect of the conjugate on joint pain related behaviors were examined in the Catwalk test. HPWT, maximal contact AT and swing phase were significantly ameliorated in ACLT mice with the administration of conjugate relative to the vehicle group (Figure 6q and r).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral test data shown in Figure 6q and r.

claim: Alendronate-TβR1I conjugate relieves OA pain by modifying the disease.
source: These data suggest that alendronate-TβR1I conjugate relieves OA pain by modifying the disease.
evidence: This is an inference based on the multiple beneficial effects of the conjugate on OA pathology and pain.

claim: The conjugate's pain relief effect was likely achieved by the decrease of PGE2 in the improvement of subchondral bone structure.
source: This was likely achieved by the decrease of PGE2 in the improvement of subchondral bone structure.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed reduction in PGE2 and improvement in bone structure with conjugate treatment.

claim: Surgical removal of a part of arthritic knee joint in total knee replacement can immediately relieve OA pain.
source: Since surgical removal of a part of arthritic knee joint in total knee replacement can immediately relieve OA pain (Skou et al., 2015), it is believed that peripheral input is indispensable in OA pain sensitization.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous clinical work.

claim: Peripheral input is indispensable in OA pain sensitization.
source: Since surgical removal of a part of arthritic knee joint in total knee replacement can immediately relieve OA pain (Skou et al., 2015), it is believed that peripheral input is indispensable in OA pain sensitization.
evidence: This is an inference based on the clinical observation that removing the joint relieves pain.

claim: Synovium is thought to be one of the important sources of OA pain because of its dense innervation of sensory nerves.
source: Synovium, because of its dense innervation of sensory nerves, is thought to be one of the important sources of OA pain (Kc et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Synovial sensory nerve declined in some of the degenerative OA patients.
source: However, human studies showed that synovial sensory nerve declined in some of the degenerative OA patients (Dominique Muschter et al., 2017; Sellam and Berenbaum, 2010), making this hypothesis inconclusive.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The increase of vascular and nerve growth in meniscus suggests that it might be a source of pain.
source: Similarly, the increase of vascular and nerve growth in meniscus (Ashraf et al., 2011) and fat pad (Bohnsack et al., 2005) suggests that they might also be a source of pain.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The increase of vascular and nerve growth in fat pad suggests that it might be a source of pain.
source: Similarly, the increase of vascular and nerve growth in meniscus (Ashraf et al., 2011) and fat pad (Bohnsack et al., 2005) suggests that they might also be a source of pain.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Subchondral bone marrow lesion (BML) strongly correlates with knee pain in humans.
source: Subchondral BML is the first sign of OA in animal models (Libicher et al., 2005) and strongly correlate with knee pain in humans (Davies-Tuck et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous clinical work.

claim: Subchondral BML is the first sign of OA in animal models.
source: Subchondral BML is the first sign of OA in animal models (Libicher et al., 2005) and strongly correlate with knee pain in humans (Davies-Tuck et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Perivascular sensory and sympathetic nerve fibers breach the subchondral bone in OA compared to normal joint.
source: Studies have showed perivascular sensory and sympathetic nerve fibers breach the subchondral bone in OA compared to normal joint (Mapp and Walsh, 2012; Walsh et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The development of OA pain is a synergistic result involving central sensitization in spinal cord in conjunction with peripheral input from subchondral bone, synovium, meniscus and fat pad.
source: Taken together, we believe that the development of OA pain is a synergistic result involving central sensitization in spinal cord in conjunction with peripheral input from subchondral bone, synovium, meniscus and fat pad etc.
evidence: This is an inference based on the authors' synthesis of the evidence.

claim: Neuronal plasticity including activation, transcriptional modification and post-transcriptional of ion channels related to electrical excitability could contribute to the generation of chronic pain.
source: It is widely accepted that neuronal plasticity including activation, transcriptional modification and post-transcriptional of ion channels related to electrical excitability could contribute to the generation of chronic pain (Woolf and Salter, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Pain sensation and OA progression are often dissociated.
source: Pain sensation and OA progression are often dissociated.
evidence: This is based on clinical observations discussed in the manuscript.

claim: Late stage of radiographic OA patients with extensive subchondral bone sclerosis may result in less pain sensation.
source: Late stage of radiographic OA patients with extensive subchondral bone sclerosis may result in less pain sensation and early stage patients with significant subchondral BML can be very painful.
evidence: This is based on clinical observations.

claim: Early stage patients with significant subchondral BML can be very painful.
source: Late stage of radiographic OA patients with extensive subchondral bone sclerosis may result in less pain sensation and early stage patients with significant subchondral BML can be very painful.
evidence: This is based on clinical observations.

claim: The anti-nerve growth factor (NGF) tanezumab administration to OA patients relieves pain with no significant attenuation on OA cartilage protection or subchondral bone sclerosis.
source: Moreover, the anti-nerve growth factor (NGF) tanezumab administration to OA patients relief pain with no significant attenuation on OA cartilage protection or subchondral bone sclerosis (Lane and Corr, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous clinical work.

claim: Although pain relief can be achieved to some extent by targeting NaV1.8, the cartilage or subchondral bone was not significantly protected in OA progression after ACLT.
source: Consistently, although pain relief can be achieved to some extent by targeting NaV1.8, the cartilage or subchondral bone was not significantly protected in OA progression after ACLT in our study.
evidence: This is supported by the manuscript's own data from the NaV1.8 ablation experiments.

claim: A comprehensive therapy for OA should target upstream events that cause OA progression and pain.
source: These results indicate a comprehensive therapy for OA should target upstream events that cause OA progression and pain.
evidence: This is an inference based on the dissociation between pain relief and disease modification.
